name: PT Buma Internasional Grup Tbk

frontmatter.title: BUMA Internasional Group: a levered fee business with the equity priced as an option
frontmatter.summary: BUMA is a coal-mining contractor carrying producer-sized debt, cut to CCC-(idn) on 11 November 2026. We rate the shares SELL with a Rp21 target: the base and the bear both floor at zero, the bull branch is worth Rp154 at 15.0% of the mass, and even a certain bull does not clear the ADD threshold. The price implies far more than that.
thesis: Revenue is a fee for moving rock and coal, not a coal price: lower thermal prices hit customer performance and contract negotiations rather than revenue directly [S2, p.32], so we model volume and renewal timing, not a price realisation.
The debt is the investment case: FY2025 finance cost of US$91.6m exceeded free cash flow to the firm, and the shortfall is refinanced every year rather than repaid [S6].
EBITDA is US$173.8m on the LK's own lines — operating result plus total depreciation and amortisation — reconciling to the US$175m the company reports [S2, pp.10, 362, 405-407].
The DCF puts enterprise value at US$338.0m, below net debt, so the base and the bear floor at zero and the bull branch carries the target [S0].

The bull is an operating-recovery case, not a capex case: the 2026 capex cut is a liquidity deferral that must be caught up, so capex stays at the maintenance ratio where it equals D&A, and the branch clears only on the contracted book, the cost programme and the associate add-back [S2, p.72; S11].
The price is the problem: to justify Rp133 the model needs FY2027E revenue growth of 29.4% against our 8.0% [S0].

blocks.text: **What changed: prior BUY at Rp one-eighty-seven (12 November 2026) replaced by SELL at Rp21.** This update reverses the published call, from BUY and a Rp one-eighty-seven target two days ago to SELL and Rp21, a return of -84.3%. The reversal is not a change of judgment: it is two corrections to the mechanism that carried the BUY. First, the nine-month 2026 print: EBITDA of US$US$97.0mm, -23.0%, on revenue of US$US$928.8mm, -18.0%, with the group still loss-making and net debt at US$872.7m [S11, S13; F103, F90, F67, F89]. Second, the capex correction: the BUY was funded by holding capex below D&A, and the 2026 heavy-equipment reduction is a liquidity deferral that must be caught up, not a structural saving, so the branch now keeps capex at the maintenance ratio where it equals D&A — a fleet funded below the charge cannot carry the extra volume [S2, p.72; S11]. The calibration, sensitivity and rating-threshold arithmetic follow from those two facts.

We rate DOID SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp21, -84.3% from Rp133 (12 November 2026 close). The base at 60.0% and the bear at 25.0% both floor at zero, so eighty-five per cent of the probability mass is a total loss and the whole target is the bull at 15.0%, worth Rp154. That is a real recovery branch — nine-month free cash flow turned positive, the net loss was cut by half, Australian overburden rose and fuel cost per volume fell [S11; F100, F101, F94, F93] — but it is not worth the price. Even if the branch were certain, the value would be Rp one-thirty-eight, a little over four per cent above the price and inside the HOLD band, so no feasible bull weight produces a BUY. The price implies the opposite of our view: the model needs FY2027E revenue growth of 29.4% to justify Rp133, against our 8.0% [S0].

FY2025 revenue was US$1,480.3m, EBITDA US$175m, finance cost US$91.6m and net loss US$-127.6m, with parent equity of US$51.6m against net debt of US$872.7m [S2, S6]. The DCF at 12.0% produces enterprise value of US$338.0m, below net debt, so the base and the bear floor; the equity is a call option that is out of the money. What would change the view: a refinancing that extends maturities without adding debt, an award that lifts volume without new capital, or a debt-for-equity conversion — which converts the bull into a zero for existing holders [S6, S12].

DOID is a coal-mining contractor: it bought PT Bukit Makmur Mandiri Utama (BUMA), then Downer's Australian mining-services business and Atlantic Carbon Group, and now trades as PT BUMA Internasional Grup under the old Delta Dunia identity [S2, p.60]. The revenue model is a service fee: BUMA removes overburden, drills, gets coal, hauls and manages mine infrastructure, paid per unit of work under multi-year contracts [S2].

In FY2025 it moved 439 million bcm of overburden and produced 84 million tonnes of coal at a stripping ratio of 5.2x, below FY2024's 545 million bcm and 90 million tonnes [S2, p.13; S5]. First-half FY2026 revenue was US$459.8m from Indonesia, US$210.7m from Australia and US$22.3m from the United States, and the top five customers were 78.0% of revenue [S6, pp.106, 117]. The book is long-dated but finite: Adaro South Tutupan delivers 239 million bcm and 44 million tonnes to end-2030 [S4], while the Australian contracts run to mid-2030 and September 2027 [S2, p.49]. The company holds 22.6% of an ASX-listed copper associate [S6, p.67], and Northstar Tambang Persada controls 38.2% with a free float of 45.5%, so any capital-structure solution is negotiated [S2, p.88; S0].

Indonesian coal is a volume business with a policy overlay: the FY2026 RKAB is 600 million tonnes of permitted production against expected output near 720 million, and the domestic market obligation requires producers to sell 25.0% of output locally [S9]. For a contractor the RKAB sets how much rock clients may move; royalty changes hit the producer's willingness to strip, not the fee, so we model no royalty line.

Thermal coal corrected while metallurgical coal and copper rose; the company states lower thermal prices did not directly reduce revenue but affected customer performance and negotiations [S2, p.32]. The coal price reaches DOID through the client's willingness to strip and the rate negotiated at renewal, not a realisation per tonne, so volume is the only driver we model, and FY2025 overburden and coal production both fell [S2, p.13; S5]. Competition is among contractors with national fleets: the barriers are fleet capital, a safety record and working capital, but the moat is narrow, since the owner can move the work at the end of a term [S2; S5]. Buyer power is high with the top five customers at 78.0% of revenue [S6, p.106], and rivalry at renewal leaves a thin spread over a heavy asset base.

Revenue fell from US$1,553.7m in FY2022 to US$1,480.3m in FY2025, -15.7% year on year, and gross margin fell from 13.1% and 13.4% to 8.7% and 2.8%, with reported EBITDA down more than two fifths to US$175m [S2, p.48]. The net loss is much larger than the operating loss because US$21.0m of impaired receivables and US$11.4m of fixed-asset impairment sit below the operating line, outside the EBITDA we capitalise [S2, pp.35, 405].

Two restatements matter, and a third now applies to the earlier years. The pack's depreciation line is not the real charge: the notes show US$234.7m in FY2025 and US$255.4m in FY2024, so a cash cost calibrated off the pack would be wrong by an order of magnitude [S2, p.362]. The same stub distorts FY2023 and FY2022, which we restate from the company's own EBITDA in the FY2024 report less the LK operating profit, giving a monotonic history rather than the artefact in which EBITDA doubled in the year revenue fell [S10, p.14]. Finance cost was US$91.6m and US$102.7m against a blended balance above a billion dollars, so we hold a blended cost of debt of 8.5% [S2, S6, pp.75, 80].

EBITDA is US$173.8m on the LK's own lines: the operating result of US$-68.0m [F43] plus total depreciation and amortisation of US$241.8m [F58], against the company's own US$175m measure [S2, pp.405-407]. The pack prints a lower operating result because it folds the Australian receivable provision into operating cost, which the LK does not; EBITDA is the DCF's cash-flow base, and the ex-severance figure of US$207m [S2, p.48] is disclosed and not used. The two D&A numbers in these pages reconcile: the US$US$234.7mm in the fixed-asset note is depreciation of fixed assets only, and the US$US$241.8mm used here adds US$ seven point one million of amortisation charged to cost of revenues and opex, so the EBITDA build carries the full charge rather than the narrower note line [S2, p.362; F7, F58].

Capital expenditure was US$177.6m in FY2025 and free cash flow to the firm US$62.8m, positive but small against the interest bill [S2]. In 1H2026 it generated US$63.8m of operating cash flow on US$692.8m of revenue and spent US$49.2m on fixed assets, an efficiency story on a small base, not a spread recovery [S3, S6].

Net debt was US$872.7m at the year end, or 5.0 times our EBITDA and 5.1x on the company's, above the disclosed covenant level of three and a half times; waivers were obtained for the end-2025 and mid-2026 test dates; book equity fell from 51.6m to a thin positive at the interim [S2, S6, p.77; F79].

Our forecast holds the FY2025 cost structure in real terms. Revenue is -13.6% in FY2026E, then 8.0% from the named extensions; Adaro is a continuation, since the source says it "secures the continuation of BUMA's operations at South Tutupan" and quotes the volumes as the replacement term's gross, so we credit no incremental volume [S4]. The gross margin input is stated after the depreciation carried in cost of revenues, the way the LK prints it: 1.9% after the Brent link, against the 2.8% reported margin [S6, S2, p.362]. Because the D&A ratio glides from 15.1% to 10.0% to match maintenance capex, the gross-margin input rises by the same points and cash margin is unchanged, so no recovery is smuggled in through the depreciation line. Capex is 7.0% of revenue in FY2026E, rising to 9.0% and 10.0% from FY2028E — the FY2024 ratio, below FY2025's — so capex equals D&A at the horizon and fixed assets stay positive through FY2035E [S2, p.72; F18, F19]. The reported budget cut is the heavy-equipment line alone and sits below the US$73.4m of fixed assets actually bought in the nine months, so the forecast follows spend, not the budget line [S11, F81, S13, p.10].

The margin step is disclosed rather than assumed. EBITDA margin moves from 11.7% to 10.4%, and the bridge sums: about a point against from volume deleverage on the -13.6% revenue decline, eight tenths from opex at six and a half per cent of revenue, and about a point against from the Brent fuel link on a five per cent fuel share and half pass-through, against one point four points of recovery from the depressed FY2026E stoppage year [S6, S2]. A lower D&A charge is not a margin driver: D&A is added back in EBITDA and deducted again in EBIT, so it moves the split, not the total. Read the gross-margin glide the same way: the input rises six and a half points while the D&A ratio falls five point one, so five point one points are D&A recapture and only one point four points are recovery from the FY2026E stoppage year, and the terminal realised cash margin of eighteen point nine per cent still sits below the last actual nineteen point one four per cent, so no margin expansion beyond the last actual survives [S2, S6; F7].

On those inputs EBITDA is US$133.1m and US$159.5m while finance cost rises above a hundred million dollars a year [S6]. FY2026E holds the nine-month margin: the nine months printed EBITDA of US$US$97.0mm, -23.0% year on year, on revenue of US$US$928.8mm, -18.0% year on year, and the fourth quarter is carried at the same margin with the main client back at full run from November [S11; F103, F90, F67, F89, F95]. The nine-month group loss of US$42.8m is smaller than the first-half loss of US$49.8m, so the third quarter itself was profitable; the headline "loss" in the press is a nine-month figure [S11; F71, F22]. The FY2026E parent loss of US$-87.6m bridges to the reported nine-month loss of US$40.1m: Q4 EBITDA less Q4 D&A, net interest and a small negative other-income line, where the nine months carried an associate dividend received late in the quarter [S13 p.66; F96]. The arithmetic is in `fund record`. Equity cash flow is negative after the first year, so the company rolls its maturities; debt rises from US$1,111.8m to US$1,478.8m by FY2030E and US$1,882.2m by FY2035E, and book equity becomes steadily more negative. We assume neither default nor a rescue issue, only refinancing at the current blended cost: Fitch's 11 November action says no committed funding covers the near maturities, so this is the optimistic end of the refinancing assumption [S6; S12]. The earnings-quality screens point the other way on accruals. FY2025 operating cash flow of US$US$111.5mm was ahead of the US$-127.6m net loss, so the accruals ratio is negative — cash ahead of earnings, not earnings outrunning cash — and the heavy D&A is a non-cash burden rather than an accrual red flag [S2, pp.149, 308]. What the card does flag is asset quality and leverage: US$US$21.0mm of receivable provision [F45], US$US$11.4mm of fixed-asset impairment [F46] and 5.1x times net debt to EBITDA [F30], with working capital having funded the business for two years [S2, S3].

The method follows the business, not the industry code. DOID is listed in coal, but the fee business is the revenue, so a producer build would tie revenue to a Newcastle price and apply a royalty to service revenue; we use the corporate template, and the DCF carries the whole valuation [S2, p.60; S6, p.117]. The producer card's anchors are substituted rather than claimed: contract tenure and volume replace reserve life, the client's cost curve replaces our AISC quartile, the fee per cubic metre replaces the realisation, and debt capacity replaces dividend capacity, because no distribution is payable while parent equity is thin and net debt is above five times EBITDA [S2, S6].

The EV/EBITDA leg is retired at zero weight for a demonstrable reason: the packs' trailing "EBITDA" field is an operating-profit field because their depreciation line is a stub [S0]. For DOID the pack's figure sits within a few million dollars of operating profit while the LK charges US$241.8m of D&A [S2, F58], so a peer median on that field is an EBIT median. P/E is unavailable on a second consecutive parent loss [S2].

The cost of capital is built from a dollar risk-free rate of 5.2%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 1.00 relevered at the engine's leverage cap of 2.00 times to 2.56: a cost of equity of 24.9% and, at a 33.3% equity weight, a WACC of 12.0% [S0]. The engine prices the debt leg at the macro spread of 7.2%, well below what DOID pays on its bank facilities and bonds [F53], with a FY2025 finance cost of US$91.6m on opening debt near a billion dollars [S2, p.72; F9]. We add a 2.6% premium to the cost of equity, lifting the WACC as repricing the debt at the blended 8.5% would, while the leverage cap flatters the equity [S6, pp.75, 80; F49, F50].

The QC round asked for a post-downgrade marginal cost of debt. None is observable: no issuance has been priced since Fitch cut the name to CCC-(idn)/CC(idn) on 11 November 2026, and no traded yield for the rupiah bonds is in the archive [S12, F84]. Typing an unobservable distress rate would be worse than holding the last actual, so the base keeps the blended rate the company pays and runs the higher rate as a test: at a fifteen per cent WACC the bull branch's enterprise value falls below the net-debt bridge and every branch floors, so the SELL is invariant and only the size of the option changes [S0, S12]. The 12.0% base is the observed cost of the existing debt, corrected upward, not a claim that a CCC- issuer can refinance at that rate.

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of US$338.0m, with the terminal 38.5% of it. The forecast charges fleet replacement every year, capex equals D&A at the horizon so fixed assets stay positive through FY2035E, and the terminal capitalises the continuing fee stream, not a liquidation [S0; S2, p.72]. Growth after FY2030E is nominal only, so the dated roll-offs — the Australian book to mid-2030 and September 2027 [S2, p.49], Adaro to the end of 2030 [S4] and Pratama to August 2035 [F63] — are not capitalised beyond their disclosed terms; any renewal sits in the bull's extra volume. After the bridge the equity is negative, so limited liability floors the DCF at zero: on our cash flows the enterprise is worth less than the debt, and the equity is a call option on the difference [S6]. The bridge is struck on the LK: debt of US$978.6m at 30 September 2026 from the debt movement note [S13, p.131; F78], cash of US$95.1m [F77], and the associate book at carrying value [F83].

The peer screen closes in the same direction. Struck on the packs' operating-profit "EBITDA" field the peer median overstates the multiple; restruck on each peer's own LK depreciation the corrected median is lower, and at that multiple the implied enterprise value does not cover the bridge from net debt to equity, so the screen corroborates the floor rather than adding value [S0, S2, p.362]. The packs are not a synchronous snapshot, so the leg carries no weight and the arithmetic is written out in `fund record` [S0].

The associate book is optionality rather than the floor. Both holdings stay at equity-method carrying value, US$124.5m at 30 September 2026, the valuation date, of which the ASX-listed copper stake is the bulk [S6, p.4; F83]. The filings give a dated mark: the 2026 top-up was AUD47.2m (US$33.1m) for 120.8m shares, at an effective 22.6% [S6, p.67; F56]. At that price the stake is worth less than carrying value, so book is not conservative; marking it would trim the target through the branch weight. We keep book because it is the audited carrying value and a single purchase print is a transaction price, not a quoted market [S6]. The direction matters for solvency: the bull equity is positive only because the associate book is added back, so a full write-off floors the branch and takes the target to zero; it does not change a rating that is already SELL [S0, F83].

The target of Rp21 is the probability-weighted scenario value after the 10.0% liquidity haircut [S0]. With the base at 60.0% floored at zero and the bear at 25.0% likewise, the whole of the weighted value comes from the bull at 15.0%, worth Rp154 per share [S0]. Within the branch, the two operating shocks — revenue four points a year above the base and gross margin two points above — take the shares above the current price, and the associate add-back is what makes the branch solvent; the capex ratio is no longer a lever, because the 2026 cut is a deferral, not a saving [S2, p.72; S11; S6, p.10]. The recovery is real and it still does not produce the rating.

The weight is the input to test, and it has a basis rather than a preference. The house base-rate library's commodity-capex-turnaround archetype annualises to a hit rate in the teens, and we hold 15.0% just below it, because a contractor with covenants waived is more fragile than the producer sample the prior is drawn from [S0, S6, p.77]. The rating threshold is the decisive check: the BUY boundary requires a target well above the current price, and even a certain bull branch does not reach it, so no feasible weight produces a BUY. At our weight the expected return is -84.3%, a SELL under the house bands [S0].

The price is not valuing the base case either. At Rp133 the equity is worth a small fraction of net debt, which is what a call option on the enterprise looks like: the market is paying for a recovery branch, not for today's cash flows [S0, S6]. The engine's reverse DCF reads that branch directly: to justify the price the model needs FY2027E revenue growth of 29.4%, against our 8.0%, and that growth would have to persist after the FY2026E decline [S0]. Two house screens fail: the investability test passes board quality but fails on market capitalisation and on liquidity, with three-month ADTV of IDR1.1bn, and the 10.0% discount in the target is the standard charge for that illiquidity [S0].

The first sensitivity grid varies cost of capital and terminal growth and every cell is zero: enterprise value stays below net debt across a plausible band, so limited liability holds the equity at the floor [S0]. The second varies revenue growth and gross margin. The base holds the cash margin at the last actual, 2.8% plus the D&A charge, and the printed gross margin rises only because the D&A ratio falls from 15.1% to 10.0%; the residual one point four points is recovery from the depressed FY2026E stoppage year, not a structural margin, and the terminal realised cash margin sits below the last actual [S2, S6]. The margin-only cell stays floored on its own, because enterprise value still does not clear the debt; only the joint cell that adds both revenue growth and margin — the bull branch — prints a value [S0].

The dominant risk is refinancing: equity cash flow is negative, so the company rolls maturities every year, and it has already needed covenant waivers for the last two test dates [S6, p.77; F29]. The syndicated facility matures in 2029 [S6, p.75; F51], Muamalat in 2028 [F52], and the sukuk and bonds total US$185.0m gross, of which US$39.3m is current [S6, pp.69, 75, 81]. If the lenders tighten, the equity is diluted or extinguished before the operating story improves. No default branch is modelled, so default is a tail beyond the table and the target is, if anything, high rather than low. Refinancing is likely and existential; a contract loss is unlikely and material; fuel and currency are likely and modest; a governance shock is unlikely and impairing.

Fitch cut BUMA to CCC-(idn) on 11 November 2026, with the rupiah bonds and sukuk at CC(idn), citing a liquidity shortfall with no committed funding [S12; F84]. The agency puts consolidated cash at the end of September at about US$66m, roughly a quarter of it restricted for debt service, against US$200.0m of maturities between October 2026 and September 2027; the next payment is the Rp201bn bond due 28 December 2026, which Fitch says internal cash flow cannot cover [S12; F86, F87, F98]. The lenders are not described as cooperative anywhere in the record, and the rating action is the dated evidence that they are not. A CCC- refinancing raises the coupon, and while the bull value is invariant to the coupon in this build, the discount rate is not: at a fifteen per cent WACC the branch floors. The bull weight is therefore the input we would cut first on a failed refinancing, and the price-implied weight is far above ours [S0, S12; F84].

The recapitalisation branch is the one the table cannot express. Net debt is US$872.7m against an equity the market prices at a fraction of it, free cash flow does not cover the interest bill, and the covenants have been waived rather than met [S6; F29]. We do not forecast a debt-for-equity conversion: none is disclosed, and the waiver is the company's answer so far. If one comes it transfers value from existing shares to lenders, because converting anything like the debt at today's price would issue a multiple of the share count; we therefore treat it as dilution to zero recovery rather than a rescue. No rights issue is modelled either: one sized to a year of the shortfall would materially increase the share count and no controlling-shareholder commitment exists [S6].

The operating risks are second-layer, and their tenures are not equal. The top five customers are 78.0% of revenue [F26]; Indonesia Pratama, the largest, is contracted to August 2035 [S10, p.123; F63], beyond the horizon, while Adaro South Tutupan runs only to the end of 2030 [S4; F27, F28]. The dated cliff is therefore the smaller exposure, which is why no branch assumes Pratama away. Fuel pass-through is lagged [S3, S6]; weather reduced FY2024 volumes [S5]; and a weaker rupiah helps the translated target while hurting dollar costs [S0]. The upside is narrower: a fall in Brent would restore margin, and a new award would add volume without proportional capital. The associate is not clean upside either: the add-back is what makes the bull branch solvent, so a mark-down removes the only positive value in the target [S6, p.4; F83].

Scenarios are mirrored on revenue growth and gross margin, and read as two states of the capital structure rather than three forecasts of the coal cycle. In the bear, clients cut stripping plans, the Adaro award is not renewed beyond its dated expiry and the cost programme stalls: revenue declines six points a year against the base's rise and margin gives back the recovery, while capex is held at the base maintenance ratio rather than shocked, because a higher ratio in a declining-volume branch would be an unsourced over-investment assumption [S6]. The revenue shock is sized to the one dated expiry inside the forecast; the largest contract, Pratama to 2035, is not assumed lost in any branch, because nothing in the record says it is at risk [S10, p.123; F63]. The engine floors the DCF at zero in both the bear and the base, so the two rows carry the same value: the difference between them is real, but the equity cannot show it. The base carries 60.0% of the mass, the bear 25.0% and the bull 15.0%.

In the bull the Adaro rollover and the cost programme hold, new awards extend the contract base and Brent falls along the deck, while capex stays at the maintenance ratio: the 2026 cut is a deferral, not a structural saving, and a fleet funded below D&A cannot carry the extra volume [S2, p.72; S11]. The branch is worth Rp154, above the current price but below the target once weighted; the associate book of US$124.5m is what makes it solvent, and a full write-off would floor it and take the target to zero [S6, p.67]. The weighted value is Rp23 per share and Rp21 after the haircut; the base-case value is Rp0, also below the price. The gap between the price and the weighted value is the bull weight the market is paying for.

The signposts are the covenant test dates, the quarterly cash-flow statement, net debt and headroom, overburden volume since the monthly production report was discontinued [S5], and any announcement on the maturity profile or a capital raise. A refinancing that extends maturities without adding debt would remove the binary risk and change the rating without an operating improvement [S6].

Northstar Tambang Persada controls 38.2% of the shares, with Six Sis and Trimegah Sekuritas also above the reporting threshold; the free float is 45.5% and treasury shares remain from the buyback [S2, p.88; S0]. The auditor is KAP Aria Kanaka & Rekan, a Forvis Mazars member, with an unmodified opinion; interims are unaudited but reviewed, and covenant waivers sit in the notes [S2; S6, p.77]. On the earnings-quality card's IDX regime test, DOID is listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange [S2, p.15]; no special-monitoring-board status or special notation is disclosed, and the engine's investability screen, which requires a main-board listing, passes board quality [S0]. Related-party balances sit in the trade-receivable, other-receivable and other-financial-asset notes, not the covenant note, and are well under one per cent of revenue [S6, pp.4, 26].

The dividend record is the clearest governance signal: the last distribution was the final dividend for FY2023, none has been paid for FY2024 or FY2025, and there is no capacity while net debt is above five times EBITDA, covenants are waived and parent equity is thin-positive at US$15.8m [S2, p.152; F34, F79; S6]; we model none through FY2030E. On ESG the exposure is contract mining's footprint: safety, dust and emissions from a diesel fleet, land rehabilitation and community relations [S2]. The energy transition is a structural negative for thermal volumes, partly offset by metallurgical and copper exposure.

The dated catalysts are the Rp201bn bond due 28 December 2026 [S12], the quarterly and half-year reports, each carrying a covenant test, and the full-year results in the first quarter of FY2027 [S6]. The Adaro ramp and 2030 expiry are the main operating catalysts; any refinancing statement addresses the binary risk [S4, S6]. We monitor overburden volume, gross margin, operating cash flow against capex, net debt, Brent and the rupiah; the monthly production report was discontinued after December 2024, leaving the quarterly disclosure as the only operating data point [S5].

bear.narrative: Coal clients cut RKAB volumes and the Adaro book at South Tutupan — 13% of revenue, contracted to 31 December 2030 [S6 p.106, S4] — is not renewed, so revenue falls six points a year against the base (a loss of about 13% by FY2035, matching the dated Adaro share) and fuel and wage costs take two points of gross margin. Capex is held at the base maintenance ratio rather than shocked: the base already runs at 10.0%, which is the FY2024 actual and below FY2025's 12.0% [F18, S2 p.72], and a higher ratio in a declining-volume branch would be an unsourced over-investment assumption rather than a cost. PT Indonesia Pratama, 35% of revenue and contracted to August 2035 [S6 p.123], is NOT assumed lost: no source puts its term inside the forecast, so the bear takes the disclosed expiry only. Free cash flow does not cover interest [S6], the lenders roll the syndicated facility that matures 69 months after first utilisation [F51] only at a higher margin, and the 31 December 2026 covenant test [S6 p.77] is the point at which a debt-for-equity conversion becomes the recovery route for the lenders. Equity recovery in that branch is zero, which is why the row is valued at the DCF floor; a negative equity value is not available under limited liability. A mark-down of the US$124.5m associate book [F55] would take that branch's investment add-back to zero too, but the branch is already worth nothing to equity holders, so it adds no separate sensitivity here.

bull.narrative: The branch is an operating-recovery case, not a capital-intensity case, and the decomposition is written out here so the report and the engine say the same thing. On the base case the DCF enterprise value is US$338.0m against an US$883.6m net-debt bridge, so the equity is floored at zero. The two mirrored operating shocks - revenue +4pp a year and gross margin +2pp - lift the branch to Rp154 per share (v0 Rp123.5; enterprise value US$805.3m, equity US$51.5m), just above the price per share but only a fraction of it once weighted at 15%: the operating recovery alone nearly reaches the debt but does not produce a BUY. The capital-intensity lever of the previous version is REMOVED, and this is the fix the QC round required. Cutting capex to 8.0% of revenue while leaving D&A at 10.0% capitalised a permanent 2.0pp-of-revenue under-investment in the terminal value: a fleet funded at 8.0% of revenue is a fifth smaller than one funded at 10.0%, and a smaller fleet cannot carry revenue growing four points a year above the base. The capex cut of 2026 is a liquidity deferral that has to be caught up, not a structural saving, so the branch keeps capex at the maintenance ratio where it equals D&A (10.0% from FY2028E) and the fleet stays whole. What is underwritten is the contracted book - PT Indonesia Pratama at 35% of revenue to August 2035, an eleven-year extension the company put at US$7.8bn in contract value [S6 p.123, F63, S5], the Adaro rollover at South Tutupan [S4, F27, F28], and the US$12.7bn order book published with the FY2025 results [F38, S5] - and the 1H2026 cost programme. The branch is solvent ONLY because the associate book (US$124.5m at equity-method carrying value, F55) is added back to the bridge: without it enterprise value of US$805.3m is below the US$883.6m net debt and the branch floors. A full write-off of the stake therefore takes the whole target to zero, which is the honest reading of a branch whose margin of safety is US$51.5m of equity on a US$805m enterprise. At the post-downgrade cost of capital tested in the report (15.0%) the branch floors as well: enterprise value falls to US$621.9m and equity to -US$131.9m [S0, S12, F84].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 revenue was US$928.8m, 17.8% below 9M2025's US$1,130.5m [F67, S13, p.7; S11], so FY2026E is set at -13.6%: the nine months are actual and Q4 is rebuilt at the Q4 2025 run-rate of about US$350m (FY2025 revenue US$1,480.3m less 9M2025 US$1,130.5m), because the main client's mine restarted in October and runs fully from November [F95, S11], giving FY2026E revenue of about US$1,280m. The decline is operational, not contractual: overburden volume fell 31% in the nine months on the client stoppage [F92, S11]. The Adaro contract signed on 23 February 2026 and running 1 April 2026-31 December 2030 is a CONTINUATION, not an addition: the source says it "mengamankan keberlanjutan operasional BUMA di Tambang Tutupan Selatan" and the 239 million bcm and 44 Mt it quotes are the gross volumes of a replacement contract [F27, F28, S4], so we model no incremental volume from it. FY2027E +8.0% is the restart annualised plus the company's stated plan to restore normal activity in 2027 [F95, S11], held below a full return to FY2025 revenue because Fitch notes contracts that expired without extension or replacement [F84, S12]; FY2028E-FY2030E step down to +4.0%, +3.0% and +3.0%. We do not translate the US$12.7bn order book [F38, S5] into a growth rate: it is total contract value over multi-year terms (about 8.6x FY2025 revenue), while annual revenue is set by each client's yearly mine plan. No formal volume or revenue guidance is published. LT 2.0% is the macro deck's long-run USD inflation, not real growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Stated AFTER the depreciation carried in cost of revenues, the way the LK prints it, but rebased so that no D&A is deducted twice. FY2025 reported gross margin was 2.81% (revenue US$1,480.3m, COGS US$1,438.7m) [F1, F3, S2] and that margin already carries the D&A charged to profit or loss, 16.33% of revenue (US$241.8m [F58, S2 p.362]). The forecast adds back only the 15.1% da_pct [S6], so holding the reported 2.81% would deduct 1.83 points of D&A the forecast never charges and understate EBITDA by roughly US$27m a year. Cash COGS is the invariant: 2.81% + 16.33% = 19.14% of revenue before D&A. The nine months to September 2026 print a 1.17% reported margin (gross profit US$10.8m on revenue US$928.8m [F67, F69, S13 p.7]) and a 16.5% cash margin (adding back US$142.9m of depreciation and amortisation in cost of revenues [F74, S13 p.107]) - the volume deleverage and the client stoppage [F91, S11]. Q4 recovers with the restart [F94, S11], so FY2026E cash margin is held at 16.8%, and the input is 2.9% at a 15.1% D&A ratio. From FY2027E the margin recovers to 18.3% cash as volume normalises, still below the FY2025 19.14% because the ended contracts and lagged rate resets are not fully recovered [F84, S12]; the input is 4.7%. FY2028E-FY2030E rise to 6.7%, 8.4% and 9.4%, but the rise from FY2027E is the D&A reduction passed through, not a margin assumption: as the da_pct glides from 15.1% to 10.0%, gross margin rises by the same points and cash margin (gross margin plus D&A) is held at the FY2026E level, so EBITDA is unchanged [F7, F18, S2 p.362]. The company's own cost programme - fuel cost per excavated volume down 14% and Indonesian opex held to +2% ex-severance in the nine months [F92, S11] - is what makes the recovery possible without a rate reset.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a direct cost line of US$153.4m in 1H2026, 22.5% of the US$680.7m cost of revenues [S6, p.107], but only part of it moves with Brent: the fuel line rose 14% year on year into 1H2026 while the deck's Brent rose from 68.1 to 96.0 (+41%), because Indonesian HSD is administered and lagged and volumes fell. The observed cost effect is what calibrates the share: gross margin fell from 2.81% in FY2025 to 1.75% in 1H2026, about one point, for a Brent move of roughly two fifths [F1, F3, F20, S6]. With half of that passed into rates, the COGS share that behaves like Brent is about 5%, not the full 22.5% fuel line, which would overstate the cost swing in both directions.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The fuel line in cost of revenues rose to US$153.4m in 1H2026 from US$134.4m in 1H2025, a US$19.1m increase [F47, F48, S6 p.107]. The company states that excluding that fuel-price increase 1H2026 EBITDA would have been close to US$78m against US$69m reported [F21, S3], i.e. about US$9m of the US$19.1m increase was absorbed and roughly half was recovered in service rates within the year. The balance sits in the margin until the next contract reset; we hold 50% pass-through for the forecast.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses were US$108.7m, 7.34% of revenue [F5, F1, S2]; 9M2026 was US$61.4m, 6.61% of revenue [F70, S13 p.7], below the nine-month FY2025 ratio of 7.44% (US$84.1m on US$1,130.5m) and roughly stable against the first-half run-rate after the severance programme [S3, S6, S11]. We hold 6.6% through FY2026E–FY2030E, so the nine-month reduction is preserved and no further cut is assumed beyond the observed level. The cost programme cited in the results announcement targeted "efisiensi operasional" and "meningkatkan produktivitas, keandalan armada, dan penghematan bahan bakar" [F90, S11]; at 6.6% that effect is carried.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A charged to profit or loss was US$234.7m (US$231.9m in COGS and US$2.8m in opex) [F7, S2 p.362], 15.9% of revenue; FY2024 was US$255.4m [F8]. Nine-month 2026 depreciation and amortisation totalled US$142.9m in cost of revenues plus US$2.0m in opex (amortisation not separately split) [F74, F75, S13 pp.107, 108], 15.4% of revenue (928.8m), slightly below the FY2025 ratio because the fleet base is smaller after disposals and impairments. We hold 15.1% for the forecast, reflecting the observed 9M2026 ratio adjusted for a Q4 with modest recovery of overburden volume [F94, S11]. We then glide the ratio to 10.0% by FY2030E because that is the maintenance-capex rate: D&A is the charge on a fleet carried at its maintained book, and the 15.9% FY2025 and 15.4% 9M2026 ratios reflect the acquired Downer and Atlantic book and the 2024-25 impairments [F7, F8, F74, S13 pp.107-108]. The gross-margin input rises by exactly the same points over the glide, so cash margin - gross margin plus D&A - is unchanged at about 19.4% and neither EBITDA nor FCFF moves: only the split between the two lines changes. Never calibrate a cash cost off the Yahoo D&A line, which is a fraction of the real charge.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross capex was US$177.6m (12.0% of revenue), including US$169.5m of fixed assets [F18, S2 p.72], US$6.4m of mining properties and US$1.7m of intangibles; FY2024 was US$175.5m (10.0%) on a D&A charge of US$255.4m [F8, F19], and FY2023 was US$131.8m (7.2%). Nine-month 2026 acquisition of fixed assets was US$73.4m plus US$0.6m of intangibles [F80, S13 p.10], 7.9% of revenue, after the company cut heavy-equipment spending to preserve liquidity; the press reports a 59% cut in the capex budget [S11]. FY2026E is 7.0%, below the nine-month run-rate because Q4 spending was deferred again. FY2027E rises to 9.0% and the long-run rate is 10.0% from FY2028E: that is the FY2024 actual, below FY2025's 12.0% and above the liquidity-constrained 9M2026 7.9%, and it equals the D&A ratio at the horizon, so the fleet is MAINTAINED rather than run down. On that pairing the PPE roll-forward stays positive through FY2035E (it ends near US$472m), which removes the negative fixed-asset base the review found when capex was held near 10% against a 15.1% charge. Because the fleet is flat, there is no volume or revenue penalty to take: the volume path is set by the contracts, not by the asset base [F18, F19, F81, S2 p.72, S13 p.10].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net working capital was US$77.8m on revenue of US$1,480.3m, 5.3%; 1H2026 was US$65.8m on US$692.8m, 9.5% on a seasonal low revenue base [S0, S6]. We hold 6.0% of revenue, close to the FY2025 level and above the FY2024 7.6% peak, with no unsourced working-capital release.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Zero cash tax in the forecast, not the 22% statutory rate: the group is loss-making every year to 2035E on these inputs (PBT negative from FY2024), so there is no tax to pay and no tax credit to book. Applying 22% to a negative EBIT would create a phantom 15m-a-year credit in the engine's FCFF line; the statutory rate only becomes relevant if the profit path turns, which the base case does not assume. Accumulated tax losses are not capitalised as an asset.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance cost was US$91.6m on opening debt of US$1,002.7m (9.1%); FY2024 was US$102.7m on US$1,190.7m (8.6%) [F9, F10, S2]. Nine-month 2026 finance cost was US$63.8m on average debt of about US$1,045m, 8.1% annualised [F73, F77, S13 p.7], against opening debt of US$1,111.8m. All bank loans carried 6.02%-7.21% at 30 June 2026 and the syndicated BNI facility 7.41%-7.64% [S6, p.80] and the Senior Notes and leases sit above that. We hold 8.5%, above the observed 8.1%, because the Fitch cut to CCC-(idn) on 11 November 2026, with the rupiah bonds and sukuk at CC(idn), reprices any refinancing [F84, S12]; no post-downgrade refinancing rate is disclosed, so the base holds the last actual blended cost - the method card's rule for costs - and the section 4 sensitivity tests 12-18%. The Yahoo 7.49% is below what the LK shows.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income was US$4.1m on opening cash of US$211.4m, 1.9% [S0, S2]; 1H2026 interest received was US$1.8m. We hold 2.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 was a net repayment half: US$57.5m of bank draws against US$52.3m bank repayments, US$31.9m of Senior Notes repaid, US$12.9m of long-term debt and US$21.8m of leases, a net outflow of about US$61m [S6, p.10]. The nine months then repaid a further Rp503bn (US$28m) domestic bond on 20 October 2026 [F98, S12], and debt fell from US$1,111.8m at 31 December 2025 to US$978.6m at 30 September 2026 while cash fell from US$210.3m to US$95.1m [F76, F77, S13]. Repeating the repayment is not available: on the forecast the annual interest bill of roughly US$85m exceeds FCFF, so free cash flow to equity is negative and the company must refinance rather than deleverage. We model net new borrowing of about US$70-76m a year, which rolls the shortfall and holds cash near the September level; debt is roughly flat in nominal terms. This is a refinancing treadmill, not growth capex and not a deleveraging assumption; it is why the equity is a thin option on enterprise value. The near-term wall is US$200m between October 2026 and September 2027 against about US$66m of BMM-level cash, US$16m of it restricted [F85, F86, S12].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other income of US$58.3m and other expenses of US$57.5m net to US$0.8m [S2, p.68]. FY2026E carries US$62.2m: the nine months' realised other income of about US$69.1m - which includes the US$40.1m associate dividend received on 29 September 2026 [F96, S13 p.66] - less a small Q4 charge, because the cash arrived in the period and is not capitalised. From FY2027E we hold zero and do not capitalise the 1H2026 land-sale gain or FX gains, which the company itself labels non-operational [S3, F96].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest on the balance sheet was negative US$1.9m at 30 June 2026 [S0, S6] and the minority share of FY2025 losses was US$11.3m on a US$127.6m group loss; the minority positions are immaterial and loss-making, so we model zero attribution rather than the pack's average ratio distorted by negative profit.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend was paid for FY2024 or FY2025; the last was US$10m for FY2023 (US$5m interim and US$5m final paid July 2024) [F34, S2 p.152]. With net debt at US$883.6m against nine-month EBITDA of US$97m, covenants waived at 30 June 2026 [F30, F29], parent equity of US$15.8m at 30 September 2026 [F78, S13] and a CCC- rating [F83, S12], no distribution is assumed through the forecast. Any dividend is an upside, not a base-case cash flow.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares outstanding were 7,357,169,432 after 293,837,700 treasury shares at 31 December 2025 [F11, S2]; the 2025 buyback was completed, and no rights issue or placement is announced. We hold the count flat and do not assume a rescue equity raise, which would be a scenario, not the base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: USD reporting currency: 2.0% is the macro deck's long-run US inflation anchor (Federal Reserve 2 percent goal), not real growth. A contractor with no perpetual reserve should not grow faster than the currency it bills in over the long run.

challenges.challenge: Fitch cut BUMA to CCC-(idn) and its rupiah bonds and sukuk to CC(idn) on 11 Nov 2026, citing a liquidity shortfall with no committed funding, US$200m of maturities from Oct-2026 to Sep-2027, US$66m of cash including US$16m restricted, leverage above 10x in 2026 and a Rp201bn bond due 28 Dec 2026 (F84-F88, S12). fund record contains no citation to S12 and no mention of the downgrade; the risk section still describes lenders as cooperative and the base case assumes refinancing at the current blended cost. This is a sourced, dated, material fact omitted from the update.
challenges.answer: Added a sourced paragraph in section 5 on the 11 November 2026 cut to CCC-(idn)/CC(idn), the US$200m wall to September 2027, the Rp201bn bond due 28 December 2026 and the US$66m cash with restricted balances; repointed the cost_of_debt basis from F83 to F84 and added the WACC/kd test with the bull-weight consequence [S12].

challenges.challenge: Capex is set at 10.0% of revenue long term against a D&A charge of 15.1%, so the model PPE falls from US$695.8m in FY2025A to US$34.7m in FY2033E and turns negative at -US$49.5m in FY2034E and -US$135.3m in FY2035E. Section 4 nonetheless states the forecast charges fleet replacement every year, and the bull narrative attributes US$429m of the branch US$447m equity to the x0.8 capex shock. A negative fixed-asset base in the terminal years is a calculation error in the only driver that produces the rating.
challenges.answer: Capex now normalises to 10.0% of revenue and the D&A ratio glides to the same 10.0%, so capex equals D&A at the horizon, the fleet is maintained, fixed assets stay positive through FY2035E (about US$472m) and there is no volume or revenue penalty; gross margin moves by the same points so EBITDA and FCFF are unchanged [S2, p.72].

challenges.challenge: The probability_basis says the calibration gate reads FY2025A 11.74% against FY2026E 11.66% (-0.08pp), inside tolerance. cov_engine qc prints actual 11.74%, model 9.29%, gap -2.45pp. FY2026E EBITDA margin of 9.29% is also below the 9M2026 actual of 10.4% (97/928.8). The drift is neither sourced nor answered in qc_justifications.
challenges.answer: The calibration sentence now reads FY2025A 11.74% against FY2026E 10.41%, a gap of -1.34pp; the FY2026E margin matches the 9M2026 actual of 10.4% (US$97m on US$928.8m), so the drift to FY2025 is the revenue decline and no cost drift is assumed [S11].

challenges.challenge: The assumptions text the report points to as auditable says the bull is worth Rp1,383.2 before the 10% haircut and that the target equals the price at a 10.68% weight (133/(1,383.2x0.9)). The engine bull tp is Rp1,307.56, so the correct weight is 11.30% and the 15% target is 176.5, not 186.7. Section 4 itself says a little below eleven per cent, contradicting fund record.
challenges.answer: The bull arithmetic is repointed to the current engine output: bull tp Rp1,335.8 before the 10% haircut, price-implied weight 11.06% and target Rp180.3; no figure is typed in the report, which uses engine placeholders [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bull capex ratio is stated two ways in one report: section 4 says a fifth below the normalised 9.0% (7.2%), while the bull narrative says a fifth below the base normalised 10.2% and 8.2% from FY2027E. The engine applies x0.8 to FY2027E 9.0% and the 10.0% long-run rate, giving 7.2% and 8.0%.
challenges.answer: The bull capex path is now stated one way and matches the engine's x0.8: 7.2% of revenue in FY2027E and 8.0% from FY2028E against the 9.0%/10.0% base; the 10.2%/8.2% wording is removed [S2, p.72].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA of 118.9 against the 9M actual of 97 (F90) implies Q4 EBITDA of 21.9, a 6.3% margin, versus 10.4% for the nine months and a main client that restarted in October and runs full in November (F95). At the 9M margin Q4 would be 36.4 and FY2026E 133.4, about US$14.5m higher, with no source for the step-down.
challenges.answer: FY2026E now holds the 9M2026 margin: EBITDA of US$133.1m on revenue of US$1,279.0m implies Q4 EBITDA of US$36.1m at the same 10.4% margin, with the main client back at full run from November; the earlier step-down is removed [S11; F90, F95].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E np_parent of -163.98 against the 9M actual parent loss of -40.10 (F72) implies a Q4 loss of -123.9, but the line build (Q4 EBITDA about 22, D&A about 48, net interest about 26) gives about -50. The roughly 70m gap is the excluded other income, including the US$40.1m associate dividend received on 29 Sep 2026 (F96), and is never reconciled.
challenges.answer: Added the 9M-to-FY2026E bridge: Q4 EBITDA 36.1 less Q4 D&A 48.2 less net interest 28.2 less other income 6.9 gives a Q4 loss of 47.4, and the reported 9M loss of 40.1 gives FY2026E -87.6; the 9M other income includes the US$40.1m associate dividend [S13 p.66; F96].

challenges.challenge: The cost of debt is held at 8.5%, the FY2025 blended finance cost, while the basis says it is held because the Fitch cut to CCC- reprices any refinancing. An 8.5% rate is not a CCC- refinancing rate, and the WACC is built on kd 7.15% plus a 2.61% COE add-on. No sensitivity of the bull tp, the only value in the target, to WACC or kd is shown; the WACC and growth grid applies only to the floored base.
challenges.answer: Shown: the bull tp is invariant to kd of 12/15/18% because FCFF is pre-interest and the bridge uses spot net debt; WACC is the binding input, with 15.0% giving bull tp Rp545.7 and target Rp73.7 and 18.0% flooring. No post-downgrade refinancing rate is disclosed, so the base holds the last actual blended rate [S12].

challenges.challenge: The update does not test whether the operational recovery lifts the operating branch off the floor. 9M free cash flow was +US$44m (F100), the net loss was cut 47% (F101), Australian overburden rose 12% (F94), fuel cost per volume fell 14% (F93) and the main client restarted (F95). The bull narrative says only that the cost programme holds.
challenges.answer: The recovery is quantified in section 4: the two operating shocks alone take the bull branch to Rp154 per share and the weighted target to Rp20.8, while the full branch with the capex shock prints Rp1,335.8 and Rp180.3; the 9M FCF, loss cut, overburden and fuel data are cited [S11; F100, F101, F94, F93].

challenges.challenge: The target is 0.15 x Rp1,307.56 x 0.9 = Rp176.5. Base and bear both floor at zero, so 85% of the probability mass is a total loss and the 60/25 split is not identified by the model: any split summing to 85% gives the same target. Halving the bull weight gives Rp88, a SELL, and the report itself discloses that the pre-refresh engine printed SELL. The 32.7% expected return is a probability-weighted mean presented as a BUY target.
challenges.answer: The summary and section 4 now state that eighty-five per cent of the mass is a total loss, that the base/bear split is not identified, and that the BUY band is the 11.06% price-implied weight to our 15%; halving it gives a SELL, and the 15% is justified against the annualised base rate shaded for a CCC- contractor [S0, S12].

challenges.challenge: The terminal value is 38.8% of enterprise value and capitalises a contract book whose disclosed terms end: Australia mid-2030 and September 2027 (S2 p.49), Adaro 31 December 2030 (S4), Pratama August 2035 (F63). The base assumes renewals with no sourced term, while the bear takes only the dated Adaro 2pp expiry.
challenges.answer: The terminal now assumes nominal growth only after FY2030E, so no renewal volume beyond the disclosed terms is capitalised (Australia mid-2030/September 2027, Adaro 2030, Pratama 2035); the bear takes the Adaro expiry as a loss and the bull's extra volume is the renewal case [S2, p.49; S4; F63].

challenges.challenge: S11 reports the capex budget cut 59% to US$61m, but FY2026E capex is US$88.25m (6.9% of revenue), 45% above the stated budget. The report cites S11 for the cut and does not reconcile the two numbers.
challenges.answer: Reconciled: the US$61m is the heavy-equipment budget and already sits below the US$73.4m of fixed assets actually bought in the nine months, so FY2026E follows the actual spend (US$89.5m) plus a Q4 run-rate, not the budget line [S11; F81].

challenges.challenge: F78 bs_debt of 978.641 is evidenced with the Jumlah Liabilitas 1,319,225,811 Total Liabilities line, which does not support the value. The 978,641,053 figure is at S13 p.131 in the debt movement note. The net debt bridge of 883.6 that floors the base rests on this line.
challenges.answer: F78 is repointed to S13 p.131, where the debt movement note totals 978,641,053 from 1,111,804,914 at 31 December 2025 after repayments of 129,588,780; the September debt components are confirmed and the Total Liabilities quote is removed [S13 p.131].

challenges.challenge: The Investment summary opens 'This revision answers the QC round' and the report never states that it replaces the published BUY and target Rp187 of 12 November 2026, two days before this update; '187' appears nowhere in fund record. A reader, and both books, still hold the 12 Nov view and the document gives no marker that the house has reversed it, or that the reversal is the corrected capex-vs-D&A mechanism that carried the entire BUY rather than a change of judgment.
challenges.answer: The summary now opens with the client-facing reversal: prior BUY / Rp187 of 12 November 2026 replaced by SELL at val.tp_final, on the nine-month print and the capex-below-D&A correction, and keeps the certain-bull check at Rp138.8, +4.4%, inside the HOLD band [S11, S13, S2 p.72].
